pros to get their home projects done well for over 30 years. For everything from minor repairs

This is NPR News Now. The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Lakshmi Singh. President Trump is returning to Texas for a high-stakes
campaign event in San Antonio weeks before midterm election in which the GOP faces the
prospect of losing control of Congress. NPR is here and now spoke today to Laura McGaughey,
who covers Texas politics for The New York Times about what Senate candidate Ken Paxton has been
saying about the impact of Trump's low public approval numbers. There's been a number of leaks
from the Paxton camp in the last week from private events in which Mr. Paxton has said that, for
example, the big convention that they held here may have had a drag on his poll numbers and that
some public sentiment about the war in Iran and some of the Trump administration's other policies
might be hurting him at this point. Paxton is running against Democrat James Talarico,
a statehouse progressive known for invoking scripture and criticizing Republicans who've
supported Trump's policies, such as immigration enforcement and government program cuts.
A tropical storm is brewing in the eastern Gulf of Mexico. NPR's Debbie Elliott reports
its forecast to strengthen into the first hurricane of the Atlantic hurricane season.
Tropical storm Isaías formed over the western Gulf overnight. The National Hurricane Center says
it's on track to rapidly gain strength as it moves to the east over warm Gulf waters and could become
a hurricane by Thursday. Forecasters say residents from Louisiana to the Florida Gulf Coast should
be prepared for damaging winds, heavy rain, and dangerous storm surge. Florida Governor Ron
DeSantis has declared a state of emergency in 25 counties in the Panhandle and Big Bend region,
freeing up resources to be staged for a hurricane response. This year's hurricane season has been
dampened by a strong El Nino weather pattern which hinders Atlantic storm development.
Debbie Elliott, NPR News.
Russian drone and missile strikes on Kyiv in several other Ukrainian regions overnight
killed at least 21 people, including four children, and injured dozens of others.
NPR's Joanna Kakissis reports that the deadly strikes coincided
with Russian President Vladimir Putin's 74th birthday.
Writing on social media, Ukrainian President Vladimir Zelensky accused Russia's military
of deliberately targeting civilians as "a gift to Putin." Most of those killed were in
a five-story apartment building in the northern city of Priluki. This was one of the most vile
strikes Zelensky wrote. Russia is now frequently attacking with fast-moving jet-powered drones and
missiles. Ukraine is struggling to shoot them down with existing air defense systems. Zelensky is
seeking air defense supplies for immediate help while Ukraine's defense tech sector
races to develop faster and more powerful interceptors to protect Ukrainian cities.
That's Joanna Kakissis reporting. It's NPR News.
The federal government regularly surveys every public school in the United States to see if they
are upholding student civil rights. NPR's Anaki Mehta reports the latest civil rights data collection
also tells us about who is teaching those students.
The last time the U.S. Education Department collected information about teacher race,
ethnicity, and sex was in the 1970s. That changed with the latest survey about the 2023-24 school
year. The big takeaway? The teaching workforce is far less diverse than the student population.
75% of teachers are white, while only 44% of students are, and 9% of teachers are black,
while nearly 15% of students are. This matters because some research shows that a diverse
teaching workforce helps all students have better outcomes. Among other things,
the report also shows that the number of preschoolers across the nation is
rebounding from the pandemic. Jenaki Mehta, NPR News.
The German government's contending with a major blow to its security apparatus,
Esme Nicholson reports from Berlin. Former spy chief August Haning appeared in front of a
federal judge today on espionage charges and was ordered to remain in detention.
Let's be clear about the magnitude of these allegations. August Haning served as the head
of Germany's CIA equivalent, known here as the BND, for seven years. Federal prosecutors
accuse Haning of using classified information to brief a foreign intelligence agency in at
least one instance. That amounts to attempted treason, and prosecutors also believe that Haning
was in close contact with a member of another foreign intelligence agency, to whom he passed
sensitive political information. Esme Nicholson reporting. You're listening to NPR News.
